newsitem.title: USA: Clinton chides Congress on disaster aid.
newsitem.headline: Clinton chides Congress on disaster aid.

text.p: President Clinton, declaring "disaster doesn't take a holiday," Saturday criticized the Republican-controlled Congress for taking a break for Memorial Day without passing disaster aid for 33 states.

Congress recessed until June 3 without acting on legislation that would provide up to $8.4 billion in financial aid to victims of natural disasters, including the devastating floods that struck the Midwest.
"The wrath of nature can be random, swift and unforgiving," Clinton said in his weekly radio address to the nation. "That's where human nature must provide a balance."
"In government, we must act because that is our duty as Americans," Clinton said. "We cannot leave the victims without the help they need and deserve."

Clinton complained that the victims "are in dire need and Congress has failed to act for them. That is unconscionable." He urged Congress "to do its part, and to do it quickly. Disaster doesn't take a holiday."
The decision to allow lawmakers to leave Washington without passing at least some interim relief for the victims has turned into a public relations nightmare for the Republican leadership.
With such a large number of states across the nation needing disaster relief, Democrats fumed over the failure to act -- as have many state and local officials of both parties.

While Republican congressional leaders insist that the Federal Emergency Management Agency still has $2 billion it can dispense, White House officials counter that a broad range of projects -- such as repairing damaged roads and bridges -- must wait until Congress returns.

"Many members, led by lawmakers from the flooded states, worked hard to get a bill to me, but I'm sorry to say, some members of the majority tried to use this important bill for different purposes," Clinton said.
"And, without taking action, Congress left town, and our people were left in the lurch."

The president drew a sharp contrast between Congress's failure to act on the relief legislation and the bipartisan atmosphere in which lawmakers negotiated a balanced budget agreement with the White House.
"This is how our government should work," he said, pointing to disaster aid as "an example of how it should not work and how it's not working."
Clinton said tens of thousands of people who suffered losses in the Midwest floods were struggling to reclaim their lives and their communities.

"It flies in the face of the spirit of bipartisan cooperation we saw in our budget negotiations, and it's not how we treated other Americans when they were in similar dire straits over the last four years," he said.
Both parties support disaster aid, but Clinton has threatened to veto the $8.4 billion emergency measure because of unrelated spending and environmental amendments added by Republicans.

An effort to pass an interim relief bill of about $2 billion before the congressional recess began was derailed by conservative Republicans who feared it would undercut their bargaining position with the White House.

In the Republican response, Sen. Strom Thurmond, who Sunday becomes the longest-serving member of the Senate, paid tribute to those who serve in the nation's military and those who work in law enforcement.

"They are individuals who are motivated not by a desire to make money or achieve personal gain," he said, "rather, they are eager to serve others and to work to build a better and stronger United States."
Thurmond, 94, has served South Carolina in the Senate for 42 years, one-fifth of the chamber's own 208-year history.
